::: {#sol-weight-decay-sweep}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
decay_rows = []
for weight_decay in [0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1]:
    decay_net = make_net()
    decay_history, _ = fit(decay_net, weight_decay=weight_decay)
    decay_rows.append({
        "weight_decay": weight_decay,
        "train_loss": decay_history["train"].iloc[-1],
        "val_loss": decay_history["val"].iloc[-1],
        "test_accuracy": accuracy(decay_net, x_test, y_test),
    })
decay_table = pd.DataFrame(decay_rows)
best_decay = decay_table.loc[decay_table["val_loss"].idxmin()]
print(decay_table.round(4))
```

`weight_decay` $= `r py$best_decay[["weight_decay"]]`$ ends with the lowest validation loss,
`r sprintf("%.3f", py$best_decay[["val_loss"]])`,
against `r sprintf("%.3f", py$decay_table$val_loss[1])` with no [weight decay](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/regularization.html#def-weight-decay).
That is also lower than the `r sprintf("%.3f", py$best_val_loss)` that [early stopping](#def-early-stopping) reached in @sol-overfit-curves.
The largest value,
$10^{-1}$,
holds the weights so close to 0 that the network cannot fit even its training images:
its training loss is `r sprintf("%.2f", py$decay_table$train_loss[5])`.
The choice uses the [validation set](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-validation-set),
not the [test set](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-test-set),
so the test [accuracy](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/metrics.html#def-accuracy) stays a fair estimate for the chosen value.

:::
